content: The goal of integrating immunization programs with other health interventions is to enhance the coverage rates of both preventive and curative health services. Evidence from the literature demonstrates that integration can lead to improved coverage, although not all studies report on both preand post-intervention coverage rates. When reported, linked interventions generally show increased coverage, though not always to the same extent as immunization coverage. For example, in the Philippines, a strategy called EPI+ integrated family planning and vitamin A supplementation into routine immunization services at outreach sites. After one year, the coverage of fully immunized children increased from 80% to 90%, the utilization of family planning services by mothers of infants rose from 70% to 80%, and infant vitamin A supplementation coverage improved from 70% to 90%. Similarly, in the Congo, an immunization campaign initially faced low parental support due to the perceived lack of immediate benefits from the polio vaccine. However, participation increased when deworming tablets were added to the campaign, as the community observed immediate and visible effects from the deworming intervention. Integrated health services offer several benefits, such as more efficient use of resources (e.g., trained health workers, transportation, and logistics), increased convenience for service users by reducing the number of visits required, reduced missed opportunities for care, and improved community acceptance of the interventions. However, there are also risks and challenges associated with integration. For instance, delivering multiple interventions can increase the time required for service delivery, potentially overburdening health workers and negatively affecting their morale. Logistical challenges, such as stockouts of vaccines or supplies, can also jeopardize the success of integrated programs. Integration may reduce stigma associated with accessing certain services, such as HIV care or family planning, thereby improving access. However, it could also inadvertently reduce demand for immunization services if stigma surrounding integrated services affects community perceptions. In Madagascar, during a Child Health Week, the addition of HIV testing and family planning counseling to childhood immunization services significantly increased the time required for service delivery compared to vaccination alone, slowing the overall process. In Liberia, a project integrating family planning and immunization highlighted the importance of ongoing monitoring and adjustments during implementation. Preparatory research identified challenges such as stigma associated with mothers seeking family planning services and a lack of privacy at immunization stations. These issues were addressed by introducing privacy screens, improving commodity supply chains, and encouraging better communication and coordination among service providers. Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) are critical for integrated health services to track progress, identify areas for improvement, and assess impact. Effective M&E can enhance understanding of what works and what does not in integration efforts. Existing monitoring systems should be utilized wherever possible to minimize resource demands. For example, immunization monitoring tools can be adapted to include additional service delivery data, such as family planning or malaria prevention services. Integrated service delivery should be routinely monitored for changes in service delivery, coverage, equity, and quality of care. Monitoring service delivery separately from coverage is important, as it can reveal whether more beneficiaries are receiving care and whether integrated services are consuming more or fewer resources. Data sources for service delivery measures should ideally come from existing systems, such as health facility registers, tally sheets, and monthly reports. In some cases, it may be possible to incorporate immunization measures into the monitoring of other integrated services, particularly if those services already have strong monitoring mechanisms in place. For example, integrating birth-dose vaccination into newborn or postnatal care could benefit from the robust monitoring systems of those services.
